title: Private deployments: VPC & on-prem deployment guide, day-2 ops, upgrade and rollback, customer requirements
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's recommended approach for private deployments (VPC and on-prem), including reference architectures, packaging guidance, an operational Day-2 checklist, detailed upgrade and rollback procedures, and a customer requirements library. It is intended for solutions engineers, site reliability engineers, and deployment engineers executing or supporting private deployments for customer-managed environments.

Goals
- Provide a repeatable, low-risk deployment and upgrade path for VPC and on-prem customers.
- Define Day-2 operational practices (monitoring, backups, scaling, incident response).
- Standardize customer requirements for networking, security, hardware, and compliance.
- Document tested rollback and mitigation steps to meet SLA commitments.

Summary recommendations (TL;DR)
- Use the control-plane-hosted model when customers accept managed control plane; otherwise deploy the private control plane with the redwood-operator.
- Standard reference architecture: control-plane (optional), private-agent fleet (k8s or bare-metal), model-runtime pods, KV cache layer, ingress + service mesh.
- Enforce private KMS/HSM integration for key material.
- Upgrade via canary -> staggered rolling -> validate -> promote; rollback immediately on key validation failures.

1) Reference architectures (high level)

Architecture A: VPC-hosted control plane + customer-managed data plane
- Components: redwood-control-plane (SaaS), redwood-agent (EKS/GKE/AKS), model-runtime (GPU nodes), model-store (S3-compatible), redis-kvcache (managed), metrics collector (Prometheus), tracing (Jaeger)
- Networking: Private subnets for runtime, NAT for control-plane egress, VPC endpoints for object storage, security groups with least privilege
- Use case: customers who want SaaS control plane but require data plane isolation and dedicated GPU capacity

Architecture B: Full private (air-gapped / on-prem)
- Components: redwood-operator (k8s operator), private-control-plane (customer-managed), model-runtime (GPU nodes with container runtime), object-store (NFS or on-prem S3), redis-kvcache (HA), internal load balancer, optional service mesh
- Networking: No public egress by default; configure bastion + jump hosts for maintenance; enforce egress policies with allowlists
- Use case: regulated environments, air-gapped deployments

Diagrams
- See diagram assets in the deployment artifacts folder (link provided in handoff). Diagrams include: network zones, control-plane interactions, model shard placement, and KV cache topology.

2) Pre-deployment checklist (customer-facing)

Please present the following checklist to customers prior to scheduling delivery. The table below is represented as bulleted requirements for copy/paste into statements of work.
- Contact and roles: primary infra contact, security lead, on-call escalation list
- Networking: CIDR blocks for runtime and control plane, firewall and proxy details, NAT/egress rules, required VPC endpoints (S3, ECR, artifact registry)
- Identity & Access: Customer KMS/HSM integration plan, service account naming conventions, RBAC boundaries
- Hardware: GPU type and count (recommended: A100 or H100), minimum 8 CPU and 64GB RAM per host for small runtime nodes, NVMe recommended for model cache
- Storage: object store endpoint and credentials, snapshot plan for persistent volumes, backup retention policy
- Compliance: data residency requirements, audit logging requirements, approved encryption standards (TLS1.2+ at rest and in transit)
- Access for onboarding: temporary jump host or VPN access window, kubeconfig/service account for redwood-operator installation

3) On-prem packaging and installation options

Packaging approaches supported by Redwood:
- OVA / VM image for air-gapped installs (recommended for non-k8s customers)
- Helm chart + Operator for Kubernetes-based installs (EKS/GKE/AKS or on-prem K8s)
- Container images + systemd unit files for bare-metal container runtimes

Installer artifacts and checksums
- All release artifacts include sha256 checksums and signed manifests. Verify signatures against our public key or provide KMS integration for signature verification in closed environments. Example: shasum -a 256 redwood-operator-1.8.0.tgz

Helm install example (k8s)
1. Add repo: helm repo add redwood https://packages.redwood-inference/internal-helm
2. Update: helm repo update
3. Install operator (namespace redwood): helm install redwood-operator redwood/redwood-operator -n redwood --create-namespace --set image.tag=1.8.0 --set controlPlane.enabled=false

Air-gapped install notes
- Provide all container images as tarballs and the Helm chart bundle.
- Customer must provide an internal registry endpoint and credentials.
- Verify time synchronization across nodes (ntp), and supply CA bundle for TLS termination if using private PKI.

4) Day-2 operations (operational runbook)

Ownership and contacts
- Primary owner: private-deployments SRE on-call
- Secondary: solutions-engineering account lead

Standard operational runbook (daily/weekly tasks)
- Daily: check control-plane connectivity, Prometheus alerts, node GPU utilization, model-runtime pod crash loops
- Weekly: rotate short-lived credentials, verify backups, review log retention quotas
- Monthly: capacity planning meeting, upgrade candidate review, disaster recovery drill

Monitoring and SLOs
- SLOs (default customer baseline): availability 99.9% for API endpoints (control-plane-dependent), p99 response latency for text generation requests < 400ms (in-dataplane; subject to model/sequence length), token throughput goals agreed in SOW
- Key alerts: control-plane heartbeat missing > 5m, node GPU temperature > 85C, KV cache miss rate spike > 20% over baseline, OOMKills > 3 in 10m

Backups and snapshots
- Persistent volumes: daily snapshots for metadata, weekly full backups for model-store indexes
- Restore target: RTO for control-plane metadata 2h, RPO 1h for critical metadata (can be configured per contract)

Scaling procedures
1. Horizontal scaling (preferred): scale model-runtime deployment replicas, run a canary job to warm KV cache for added replicas
2. Vertical scaling: add GPUs to host (requires node drain and maintenance window); update node resource labels and redeploy scheduling rules

Log collection and support bundle
- Collect: kubectl get pods -n redwood -o wide, kubectl logs --since=1h <pod>, sudo journalctl -u redwood-runtime -n 500, promtool check rules, metrics snapshot (Prometheus /metrics endpoint), and /var/log/redwood/stack-trace.log if present
- Support bundle script: redwood-support-collect.sh --since 24h --include-metrics, produces encrypted tarball for upload to support portal

5) Upgrade strategy and validated procedure

Versioning and compatibility
- Semantic versioning of operator, control-plane, and runtime components. Cross-check compatibility matrix in release notes before upgrade.

Pre-upgrade checks (must pass before starting)
- All pods in redwood namespace in Ready state
- No critical alerts firing for 30m
- Recent successful backups (metadata snapshot within RPO)
- Sufficient spare capacity (at least 20% headroom)

Canary upgrade pattern (recommended)
1. Prepare: upload new images to registry, update Helm values file with new image tags and any config changes
2. Canary: upgrade operator in a single dedicated namespace or a single node group with --set canary=true; run smoke tests (health checks, simple generation, embedding) for 30 minutes
3. Validate: collect perf metrics, compare p99 latency and error rates against baseline (automated tests)
4. Gradual rollout: if canary passes, perform staggered rolling upgrades across node pools (10-25% of nodes per batch)
5. Finalize: run full integration tests, clear feature flags if any, promote new manifests to stable channel

Post-upgrade validation checklist
- Control-plane and agent heartbeats normal for 15m
- No regression in p99 latency > 10%
- Error rate for generation calls < 0.5% increase over baseline
- KV cache warming successful for major models

6) Rollback procedure (validated, low-latency rollback)

When to rollback
- Canary or batch shows p99 latency regression > 20% or error rate increase > 2%
- Failed migrations or incompatible operator behavior

Rollback steps (safe rollback pattern)
1. Pause rollout: disable further batches and set maintenance flag on control-plane to block traffic to upgrading nodes
2. Revert manifests: helm rollback redwood-operator <previous-release> or apply previous Kubernetes manifests
3. Drain and restart: drain nodes running new runtime pods, restart previous-version pods with imagePullPolicy=IfNotPresent to avoid pulling newer images
4. Validate: run smoke tests and check core SLOs for 20 minutes
5. Investigate root cause offline and open a postmortem; do not reattempt upgrade until causes are mitigated

Emergency immediate rollback (if degradation is severe)
- Route traffic away: update service routing (ingress or service mesh) to point to previous deployment flavor or standby fleet
- Feature-flag out breaking change
- If control-plane is impacted, enable customer fallback to a compatible stable API endpoint documented in the SOW

7) Upgrade rollback runbook for DB and schema migrations

Principles
- All migrations must be reversible or have compensating migrations documented
- Migrations should be feature-flag gated; run non-blocking migrations first

Procedure
1. Backup DB and metadata snapshot before running migrations
2. Run schema migrations in a canary namespace or with a small subset of tenants
3. Validate read/write operations and run reconciliation jobs
4. If migration fails, run documented revert script and restore DB from snapshot if necessary

8) Customer requirements library (standardized checklist)

Network & Security
- Allowlist: control-plane API ranges (provided per-deployment), outbound access to artifact registries, and NTP time servers
- TLS: mutual TLS for control-plane <-> agents, customer-provided CA for on-prem where required
- Auditing: syslog or centralized audit endpoint with 365-day retention option

Hardware & Capacity
- Recommended GPU types: H100 or A100 (8+ per cluster recommended for production), GPU memory sizing based on largest model tokens in flight
- Disk: NVMe for model cache, RAID1 for OS volumes, separate PV for model-store with 99.9% durability SLA

Identity & Key Management
- KMS/HSM: provide endpoint and service principal for key usage; ensure usage logs are forwarded to central SIEM
- RBAC: Kubernetes role model for redwood-operator and operators' service accounts

Compliance & Data Residency
- Data-handling policy, retention windows, and purge processes to match customer policy
- Evidence: enable audit logging and provide export for compliance evidence requests within 48 hours

Operational SLAs and Support
- Onboarding window: 4-8 weeks depending on packaging and approvals
- Support tiers: Standard (business hours), Premium (24/7 with 1h response for sev-1)

9) Handoff artifacts and delivery checklist

Delivery artifacts to provide to customer at handoff:
- Helm chart bundle and signed manifests
- Support bundle and collection script
- Deployment runbook (this document) and escalation contacts
- Post-deployment test suite (automated smoke tests and perf tests)

10) Troubleshooting quick reference

Symptom: control-plane heartbeat missing
- Check: control-plane pod logs, agent logs for TLS handshake errors, firewall/NAT rules blocking egress
- Fix: restart agent with increased log-level, re-provision temporary creds, or open support ticket if root cause is control-plane certificate rotation

Symptom: p99 latency spike after upgrade
- Check: model-runtime pod restart counts, GPU saturation, KV cache miss rate
- Fix: rollback to previous runtime image, increase batching config, warm cache using synthetic traffic

Ownership and escalation
- L1: on-call infra engineer (customer-facing)
- L2: private-deployments SRE
- L3: runtime / kernel team (contact list in handoff bundle)

Appendix: useful commands and snippets
- kubectl commands for common checks: kubectl get pods -n redwood, kubectl describe pod <pod> -n redwood
- Support bundle: ./redwood-support-collect.sh --since 24h --output /tmp/support.tgz
- Helm rollback example: helm rollback redwood-operator 2 -n redwood
